domain: OVERLOOKED PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRIES NOT TRADITIONALLY SERVED BY SOFTWARE
title: Independent pharmacies are reimbursed below acquisition cost on a large share of generics and cannot efficiently prove or contest it
affected_user: Owner/pharmacist-in-charge of an independent community pharmacy (roughly 18-19k US stores per NCPA), especially in rural areas
job_to_be_done: Dispense prescriptions profitably, identify which claims are paid below NADAC/acquisition cost, and contest or decline those claims (where state law allows) before the quarter's margin is gone
current_process: PBM adjudicates each claim in real time against an opaque MAC list; the pharmacy sees reimbursement per claim but must manually reconcile it against wholesaler invoices and NADAC; appeals go through per-PBM MAC appeal portals with short windows; DIR/clawback effects show up weeks-months later; new cost-plus contracts require sending confidential wholesaler invoices to the PBM to prove acquisition cost
what_fails: Reimbursement lands below cost on a large fraction of claims and the owner only finds out after reconciliation; MAC appeals are per-claim and labor intensive; clawbacks and delayed payments hit cash flow; cost-plus contracts demand invoice disclosure to a PBM that often owns a competing chain
failure_frequency: NCPA Jan 2025 member survey: 40.8% of independents paid below NADAC on more than 40% of Medicare Part D scripts; 29.2% below NADAC on 50% or more. Drug Topics (2026): 30.3% of owners considered closing in 2025.
cost_of_failure: NCPA: 80.3% said financial health declined in 2024 (48.6% significantly); 96.5% said PBM/Part D reimbursement threatens viability; NCPA Jan 2026 flyer ties closures to delayed payments, clawbacks, below-cost reimbursement and cites $7.3B PBM markup revenue 2017-2022. Per-store dollar loss not found.
existing_workaround: Declining to stock drugs (93.2% have decided or are considering not stocking Medicare negotiated-price drugs); refusing to fill specific scripts in states with below-cost refusal rights (e.g., Oklahoma); joining PSAOs/buying groups; state-by-state lobbying for acquisition-cost floors (Colorado HB 25-1222 effective 2026-01-01, Mississippi House bill 2026)
who_pays_today: Pharmacy owners (staff reconciliation time, PSAO fees, reconciliation/DIR-tracking vendors), NCPA dues, state legislatures' enforcement budgets

sources.note: NCPA member survey: 40.8% paid below NADAC on >40% of Part D scripts; 96.5% say reimbursement threatens viability; 80.3% financial health declined.
NCPA flyer linking closures to delayed payments, clawbacks, below-cost reimbursement; $7.3B PBM markup revenue 2017-2022.
Trade press at NCPA 2026: underwater generics and opaque MAC remain top threat; cost-plus contracts require sharing wholesaler invoices with PBMs that own competing chains.
30.3% of independent owners considered closing in 2025.
Law-firm summary: 2026 federal PBM provisions do not mandate acquisition-cost-plus-fee reimbursement, so below-cost claims continue.

firsthand_evidence: Survey respondents (NCPA, Jan 2025) report being paid below NADAC on most of their Part D volume and say reimbursement threatens the viability of their business; at NCPA 2026 owners described being asked to hand confidential wholesaler invoices to PBMs under cost-plus contracts and worried the PBM's affiliated chain would see their costs. No Reddit r/pharmacy thread surfaced in results.
key_unknowns: Actual 2025-2026 closure count (only vendor blogs claim 'more than one per day'); per-store dollars lost to below-cost claims; how many owners already use reconciliation software (PSAO-provided tools exist); whether owners would pay a non-PSAO third party; how fast state acquisition-cost floors change the economics
technical_unlock: NADAC is a public weekly CMS dataset; pharmacy management systems export claim-level 835/NCPDP data; combining the two with wholesaler invoice OCR enables automatic per-claim below-cost detection and batch MAC-appeal generation. Not an LLM wrapper; mostly data plumbing plus per-PBM appeal portal automation (Playwright-feasible but TOS risk).
why_now: 2026 state reimbursement floors (Colorado effective Jan 2026, Mississippi bill 2026) and refusal rights make claim-level below-cost identification actionable rather than merely informational; cost-plus contracts create a new need to prove acquisition cost per NDC; federal 2026 appropriations act PBM provisions.
existing_solutions: PSAO reconciliation tools (e.g., via buying groups), Net-Rx/Inmar reconciliation, vendor blogs from Pills2Me, EcoPharma, RxPost pitch 'survival guides'; NCPA advocacy

domain: OVERLOOKED PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRIES NOT TRADITIONALLY SERVED BY SOFTWARE
title: Owner-operators lose detention pay because brokers reject their proof of wait time
affected_user: Owner-operator and small-fleet truck drivers hauling brokered freight (spot market)
job_to_be_done: Get paid for hours spent waiting at shippers/receivers beyond the free window (typically 2 hours) stated on the rate confirmation
current_process: Driver notes arrival/departure times on the BOL by hand or asks the dock to stamp it, texts/calls the broker when waiting, then invoices detention after delivery with whatever proof they have; the broker decides whether to pay based on its own and the shipper's willingness
what_fails: Brokers deny detention citing insufficient proof (handwritten BOL note, missing notice while waiting, invoice not matching rate con, late billing, no signed BOL); drivers with timestamps and dashcam footage still get denied; contracts route disputes to arbitration; no federal rule requires detention pay at all
failure_frequency: Vendor guide citing ATRI 2024: carriers get paid on only ~55% of detention invoices sent (secondhand, unverified against ATRI). Two independent forum threads in Feb and Apr 2026 describe denials.
cost_of_failure: Unpaid 4+ hour waits per incident (per forum report); aggregate per-driver annual loss not found in results
existing_workaround: Getting dock to stamp in/out times, photographing BOL, texting broker at the 2-hour mark to create a record, refusing loads from brokers known not to pay, ELD logs as supplementary proof, vendor services that bill detention on the carrier's behalf
who_pays_today: Drivers eat the loss; some pay factoring companies or detention-billing vendors (e.g., DockPay); brokers' bond claims are impractical for detention

sources.note: Driver waited 4+ hours at receiver; broker refused because the only proof was a handwritten note on the BOL.
Driver had timestamps and camera footage; broker still said documentation was insufficient; contract has arbitration clauses.
Vendor page citing ATRI 2024 that carriers are paid on only 55% of detention invoices; lists common denial reasons.
States there is no FMCSA rule requiring brokers or shippers to pay detention; recourse depends on the rate confirmation.

firsthand_evidence: A driver on The Truckers Report (Apr 2026) said they lost detention pay again after waiting over four hours because the broker claimed a handwritten note on the BOL was not proof; another (Feb 2026) said the broker called their documentation insufficient even though they had timestamps and camera footage.
key_unknowns: True share of detention invoices denied (ATRI figure only seen secondhand); whether brokers would accept any third-party timestamp as proof; how often shipper (not broker) is the real refuser; willingness of owner-ops to pay for a proof/evidence tool versus free workarounds (ELD screenshots, photos)
technical_unlock: Phone GPS geofence arrival/departure records, timestamped photos of BOL, and automatic broker-notice emails at the free-time threshold produce a standardized evidence packet; ELD APIs (Motive, Samsara) already expose location history. Existing capability, not new.
why_now: FMCSA broker transparency rules (2026, per law-firm sources, unverified) increase carriers' right to see transaction records; soft spot market and broker failures make every unpaid accessorial more painful; 2026 forum chatter shows recurring issue.
existing_solutions: DockPay (detention billing), ELD vendor reports, factoring companies that chase accessorials, OOIDA advice on contracts

domain: OVERLOOKED PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRIES NOT TRADITIONALLY SERVED BY SOFTWARE
title: Double brokering and broker identity spoofing leave small carriers unpaid, with bonds too small to recover from
affected_user: Owner-operators and small carriers (1-10 trucks) booking loads on load boards; secondarily small brokers whose identity is spoofed
job_to_be_done: Verify that the broker offering a load is who it claims to be and will pay, before hauling; recover payment when a load turns out to be double brokered
current_process: Driver checks the MC number on FMCSA SAFER/Licensing and Insurance, looks at load board credit scores, calls the number on the rate confirmation, and hauls; if unpaid, files on the broker's $75,000 BMC-84 bond, files a complaint in FMCSA's National Consumer Complaint Database, and preserves rate cons/PODs
what_fails: Fraudsters impersonate real active brokers with lookalike email domains and phone numbers not in FMCSA records; the second broker pays reduced or nothing; bond claims are shared among many claimants so recovery is tiny; FMCSA complaint process rarely yields payment
failure_frequency: Overdrive survey: a majority of owner-operators reported encountering freight fraud or broker tricks; 28% said simple double brokering at reduced pay was most common; 23% reported being stiffed entirely by both brokers
cost_of_failure: Illustrative case: a Tennessee driver received $312 from a $75,000 bond after it was split among claimants (Yahoo/FreightWaves column). Industry-wide loss estimates ($500-700M/yr) circulate in vendor blogs without a traceable primary source.
existing_workaround: Manual MC-number/legal-name matching, checking email domain age, calling the FMCSA-listed number instead of the rate-con number, only working with known brokers, factoring companies that pre-screen brokers, carrier-vetting SaaS
who_pays_today: Carriers absorb losses; factoring companies and load boards sell vetting; broker bond/trust providers; FMCSA enforcement budget

sources.note: Overdrive reader survey: majority of owner-ops victims of freight fraud; 28% double brokered at reduced pay; 23% stiffed by both brokers.
Trade press: owner-operators are typically the ones left unpaid; double brokering has grown sharply.
Column describing a driver who recovered $312 from a $75,000 broker bond after many claimants; bond split among all claimants when broker fails.
Vendor post describing 2026 pattern of impersonating real brokers via lookalike domains and phone numbers not in FMCSA records; recommends domain-age and FMCSA-phone checks.
Load board notes FMCSA tightened financial review of broker applicants.

firsthand_evidence: A Tennessee driver, described in a 2026 column, filed on a failed broker's $75,000 bond and received $312 because dozens of other carriers had claims on the same bond. Survey respondents in Overdrive reported being paid a reduced amount by a second broker (28%) or not at all by either broker (23%).
key_unknowns: Primary source for aggregate fraud losses; how many carriers already use vetting tools (Highway, Carrier Assure, load-board scores); whether broker-side spoofing detection (domain/phone mismatch) materially reduces losses; FMCSA 2026 rule specifics could not be verified against the Federal Register
technical_unlock: FMCSA Licensing & Insurance data and SAFER are public; email-domain WHOIS age and phone-number registry lookups are cheap APIs; a rate-confirmation parser that cross-checks legal name, MC, phone, and domain against FMCSA records can flag spoofing before pickup. Existing capability; the gap is packaging for solo drivers.
why_now: 2026 FMCSA broker registration/transparency changes; load-board fraud reportedly rising post-2022; spoofing of legitimate brokers (not just fake MCs) defeats the traditional MC-number check
existing_solutions: Highway, Carrier Assure, MyCarrierPortal, CheckMyBroker.ai, Truckstop/DAT credit scores, factoring companies' broker credit checks, FMCSA NCCDB

domain: OVERLOOKED PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRIES NOT TRADITIONALLY SERVED BY SOFTWARE
title: Small home care agencies face Medicaid claim denials as states move EVV from soft to hard edits
affected_user: Owner/billing manager of a small Medicaid-funded home care or HCBS agency (personal care, home health aides)
job_to_be_done: Get paid for every visit delivered by making each claim match a validated Electronic Visit Verification record (caregiver, client, time, location, service) and the authorization on file
current_process: Caregivers clock in/out via EVV app or telephony; the agency's EVV vendor transmits to the state aggregator; billing staff manually fix exceptions (missed clock-outs, GPS out of range, wrong service code, mismatch with authorization) before submitting claims; during 'soft edit' phases claims still paid with warnings
what_fails: Under hard edits, any claim without a matching validated EVV record is auto-rejected with no payment until corrected and resubmitted; mismatches with the authorization are treated the same as missing data; states can recoup already-paid claims if EVV data cannot be produced; small agencies lack billing staff to work exception queues
failure_frequency: Vendor sources report Missouri hard edits phased from April 2026, North Carolina denying claims lacking EVV criteria, and Minnesota/Ohio/Indiana/Pennsylvania implementing hard-edit enforcement in 2026; per-agency denial rates not found
cost_of_failure: Delayed/denied revenue per visit; recoupment risk on prior claims; unknown aggregate. No primary state data found in results.
existing_workaround: Manual exception clean-up before billing, caregiver retraining, keeping paper timesheets as backup, switching EVV vendors, outsourcing billing
who_pays_today: Agencies pay EVV/agency management software vendors (CareSmartz360, ShiftCare, Caretap, etc.) and billing staff/outsourcers; states fund aggregators (Sandata, HHAeXchange, Netsmart)

sources.note: Vendor guide: 2026 nationwide shift from soft to hard EVV edits; claims without matching validated EVV record are denied.
Vendor state-by-state list: Missouri hard edits phased from April; NC denying; MN/OH/IN/PA enforcing in 2026.
Vendor blog describing EVV mismatches as a 'silent revenue killer' and recoupment risk.
Vendor blog on 2026 EVV compliance and FMAP penalty mechanics.

firsthand_evidence: None found; all 2026 results were vendor content. No agency owner complaint, appeal, or state enforcement notice surfaced in search results.
key_unknowns: Actual hard-edit effective dates (need state Medicaid bulletins); real denial rates after hard edits; whether existing EVV vendors already provide adequate pre-submission validation; the agency's willingness to add another tool on top of a mandated EVV vendor
technical_unlock: Pre-submission reconciliation of EVV export vs. claim file vs. authorization file (all structured data) can catch mismatches before the state aggregator rejects them; many state aggregators publish exception codes. Existing capability.
why_now: 2026 is when multiple states convert EVV from warning-only to claim-denial enforcement under the 21st Century Cures Act timeline
existing_solutions: EVV/agency platforms (HHAeXchange, Sandata, AlayaCare, CareSmartz360, ShiftCare, Caretap), outsourced billing firms

domain: OVERLOOKED PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRIES NOT TRADITIONALLY SERVED BY SOFTWARE
title: Child care providers wait weeks for state subsidy reimbursements and cannot track where payments are stuck
affected_user: Owners of small licensed child care centers and family child care homes that accept state subsidy (CCDF) children
job_to_be_done: Submit attendance/invoices and receive subsidy reimbursement in time to make payroll; know which claims are pending, rejected, or short-paid and why
current_process: Provider records attendance (often paper or basic app), submits monthly invoices into the state's payment portal, waits for retroactive payment (states commonly pay 30-60 days after service); errors in invoices restart the clock; providers call the agency to find out status
what_fails: New state payment systems (e.g., Montana's Best Beginnings system launched 2026) introduced delays in both subsidy payments and licensing; providers cannot predict when money arrives; state agencies lack staff to verify documentation and later claw back 'improper' payments, as a Washington audit found
failure_frequency: Montana (2026): multiple providers report delayed payments since system launch; the state says it meets the 21-day federal standard only for 'timely, error-free invoices'. Washington: auditor sampled 59 of ~400,000 monthly payments (Jul 2024-Jun 2025) and extrapolated ~$37M questionable payments; only about six auditors review payments.
cost_of_failure: Providers report risk of missing payroll and closing (Montana); state exposure of ~$37M per audit cycle in Washington, with overpayments sent for recovery from providers
existing_workaround: Lines of credit, personal savings, limiting number of subsidy children, dropping subsidy participation, repeated calls to the agency, waitlist holds on new providers
who_pays_today: Providers (float, lost revenue), state CCDF administrators (system vendors, auditors), families who lose slots

sources.note: Montana providers describe delayed subsidy and licensing payments after the new Best Beginnings system launched; one owner worries about meeting payroll.
Providers say the state's subsidy program is riddled with delays; DPHHS says it pays within the 21-day federal requirement for error-free invoices.
State auditor estimates $37M in questionable child care subsidy payments; DCYF does not check provider documentation before paying; about six auditors review payments.
Audit findings on weak oversight and missing records (signatures) in subsidy payments 2021-2024; overpayments submitted for recovery.
Vendor guide stating subsidy reimbursements commonly take up to 60 days because states pay retroactively.

firsthand_evidence: A Miles City, Montana child care owner told local TV she does not know whether state reimbursements will arrive in time for payroll since the new payment system launched; other Montana providers said the subsidy program is 'not a fallback plan' because of its delays.
key_unknowns: How many states have similar delays in 2026 (only Montana and Washington surfaced); whether the dominant failure is provider invoice errors or state processing; whether providers would pay for an invoice-validation/attendance-record tool when state portals are free; variation across 50 state systems
technical_unlock: Attendance capture with parent sign-in signatures and timestamp, automatic generation of error-free state invoice formats, and payment-status tracking; the Washington audit specifically flagged missing signature records, which digital attendance would resolve. Existing capability; main barrier is per-state portal variation.
why_now: 2026 state system migrations (Montana) created fresh delays; Washington's March 2026 audit pushes states toward documentation checks that providers must satisfy; federal CCDF rule (2024) requires prospective payment and enrollment-based payment, which states are still implementing
existing_solutions: Brightwheel, Procare, Playground, Pebble (attendance/subsidy tracking), state portals, Wonderschool

domain: OVERLOOKED PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRIES NOT TRADITIONALLY SERVED BY SOFTWARE
title: H-2A workers arrive weeks late because of multi-agency processing delays, leaving crops unplanted or unharvested
affected_user: Fruit, vegetable and row-crop farmers who rely on H-2A seasonal workers (and the farm labor contractors/agents who file for them)
job_to_be_done: Get an approved labor certification (DOL), petition (USCIS), and consular visa (State) so workers arrive on the farm's date of need
current_process: Farmer or agent files job order with state workforce agency 60-75 days before need, then DOL labor certification, then USCIS I-129 petition, then consular interview and visa issuance; each step has its own queue and no shared status view
what_fails: Workers arrive weeks after the date of need; delays occur at multiple steps (industry groups told DOL the 'real hangups' are at State and DHS); the DOL 'one-stop shop' promise has not materialized per internal emails; farmers have no recourse except complaints
failure_frequency: Texas spring 2026: farmers expected workers in February/March and were still waiting into planting season; NCAE CEO acknowledged delays stemming from several steps. Share of applications delayed not found.
cost_of_failure: Missed planting windows in Texas (Farm Progress); unverified claim of 40% Vidalia onion crop losses in Georgia (VisaVerge, single source). Per-farm dollar loss not found.
existing_workaround: Filing earlier than needed, paying H-2A agents/attorneys to chase cases, filing DOL complaints, staggering crews, planting less, using domestic labor at higher cost
who_pays_today: Farmers pay H-2A agents, immigration attorneys, and filing fees; associations (NCAE, state farm bureaus) lobby

sources.note: Texas farmers expecting workers in Feb/March 2026 still waiting; one filed a DOL complaint.
Investigative report using DOL emails: one-stop-shop effort struggled; industry says hangups are at State and DHS.
NCAE CEO acknowledges processing delays affecting Florida/Georgia growers, stemming from several steps.
Claims 40% Vidalia onion losses from H-2A delays; single less-established source, unverified.

firsthand_evidence: Texas farmers quoted by Farm Progress said H-2A crews expected in February and March 2026 had not arrived by planting; one had filed a complaint with the Department of Labor.
key_unknowns: Which step dominates delay time in 2026 (DOL vs USCIS vs consulate); share of petitions late; whether a status-tracking/filing tool can change outcomes when the bottleneck is government capacity; the agent/attorney market already handles filings
technical_unlock: Case-status scraping across DOL FLAG, USCIS case status and consular appointment systems to give farmers a single timeline and earlier warning; largely existing capability but it does not fix government processing speed
why_now: 2025-2026 federal staffing cuts and policy shifts changed processing performance; DOL announced H-2A streamlining that has not delivered; growers increasingly dependent on H-2A as domestic labor shrinks
existing_solutions: H-2A agents (masLabor, USA Farm Labor), immigration law firms, wafla and similar associations, DOL FLAG portal

domain: OVERLOOKED PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRIES NOT TRADITIONALLY SERVED BY SOFTWARE
title: Small California farms face SGMA pumping fees and reporting they do not understand and may be billed on inaccurate water-use estimates
affected_user: Small-scale and tenant farmers (often non-English-speaking, under ~100 acres) in critically overdrafted California groundwater basins
job_to_be_done: Comply with their Groundwater Sustainability Agency's allocation, metering/reporting, and fee requirements without cutting production below viability; contest inaccurate estimates
current_process: GSAs set allocations and fees, often based on remote-sensing evapotranspiration (ET) estimates or metered pumping; notices go to landowners (not tenants); farmers pay per acre-foot fees and must track usage; State Water Board probationary basins add extraction reporting and fees
what_fails: Over half of small farmers surveyed had not heard of SGMA; tenants miss GSA notices and get billing surprises; small farms pay the same per-unit cutbacks and fees as large ones; ET estimates can overstate use, producing inaccurate charges; interviewees describe cutting farms in half or more
failure_frequency: UC ANR/CAFF 2026 report: more than half of small-scale farmers surveyed had not heard of SGMA; report applies statewide across GSAs in overdrafted basins
cost_of_failure: Report authors say small farms may be unable to comply and stay in business; one interviewee described cutting the farm in half or more. Dollar figures not found.
existing_workaround: Relying on landlords for information, DWR technical assistance program, CAFF/UC Small Farms outreach, not reporting (risking penalties), fallowing
who_pays_today: Farmers (fees, lost production), DWR technical assistance program funding, GSAs' administrative budgets, nonprofits (CAFF)

sources.note: 'Managing Groundwater with Small Farms in Mind' report: first assessment of small-farm consideration under SGMA; 50 recommendations; survey finding that over half of small farmers had not heard of SGMA.
UC ANR summary: small farms may not be able to comply and stay in business; ET estimates may overstate use; tenant farmers miss GSA notices.
Regional water press coverage of the report's findings on small farms.
State Water Board 2026 resolution text excluding Tule Subbasin pumpers of 20 AFY or less from reporting requirements (adoption status not confirmed).

firsthand_evidence: Interviewees in the UC ANR/CAFF report described having to cut their farms in half or more to meet allocations; tenant farmers reported learning about GSA fees only when bills arrived.
key_unknowns: Number of affected small farms per basin; whether GSAs would accept farmer-side metering/ET data to contest estimates; language access needs; who would pay (farmers have thin margins; GSAs or DWR grants are likelier payers)
technical_unlock: Public OpenET and GSA allocation data plus low-cost flow meters let a farmer reconstruct their own water-use record and compare against the GSA estimate; multilingual notice tracking by parcel (APN) could reach tenants. Existing capability.
why_now: First-ever statewide small-farm SGMA assessment published July 2026; State Water Board probationary basin fees and reporting (Tule, Kern, etc.) ramping 2025-2026; GSAs enforcing allocations with 2040 sustainability deadline approaching
existing_solutions: DWR Underrepresented Communities/Small Farmers Technical Assistance Program, CAFF SGMA outreach (sgma@caff.org), OpenET, GSA portals, Land IQ reporting

domain: OVERLOOKED PROBLEMS IN INDUSTRIES NOT TRADITIONALLY SERVED BY SOFTWARE
title: Funeral directors cannot file death certificates until a physician signs, and chasing that signature delays burial, cremation and estate paperwork
affected_user: Funeral directors at small funeral homes, and bereaved families waiting on certified copies for burial permits, cremation authorization, insurance and bank accounts
job_to_be_done: File a complete death certificate within the state's statutory window (72 hours to 7 days) so the disposition permit issues and certified copies can be ordered
current_process: Funeral home enters demographic data into the state electronic death registration system (EDRS), then requests the attending physician complete the medical certification; many physicians are not enrolled in EDRS, are off-shift, or dispute who should sign (e.g., contract ER physicians), so the funeral home faxes/calls repeatedly
what_fails: Requests to physicians go unanswered for days (a California audit documented a funeral home submitting three requests over nine days before a signature); disputes over which physician must sign; families cannot hold services or access accounts; errors require amendment cycles
failure_frequency: Unknown nationally; California state auditor documented multi-day signature delays (fetal death context); Texas legislative analysis cited weekly complaints about signing conflicts (older)
cost_of_failure: Delayed disposition and services; family financial access delayed; funeral home staff time chasing signatures. Dollar figures not found.
existing_workaround: Repeated phone/fax follow-up, escalation to medical examiner/coroner, state medical board complaints (Louisiana board treats failure to sign as unprofessional conduct), paying for expedited amendments
who_pays_today: Funeral homes (staff time), families (delayed benefits), state vital records offices (EDRS vendors), medical boards (enforcement)

sources.note: California State Auditor report documenting physician signature delays, including a funeral home sending three requests over nine days before a physician signed.
College of American Pathologists state-by-state table: physician signing windows of 24-72 hours and filing windows of 72 hours to 7 days.
Louisiana medical board guidance: physician deadlines and discipline for failing to sign on time.
NC law-firm Q&A from a family dealing with a delayed, misspelled certificate; notes NC now requires electronic filing through NCDAVE with a five-day funeral director window.
Older Texas bill analysis citing steady weekly complaints about signing delays from disputes over which physician must sign.

firsthand_evidence: A North Carolina family asked a probate attorney (Mar 2026) how to fix a misspelled death certificate when the funeral home kept delaying; the California auditor's case file shows a funeral home requesting a physician's signature three times over nine days.
key_unknowns: National frequency of late certificates; whether EDRS vendors (e.g., state systems) already notify physicians adequately; whether the bottleneck is physician enrollment or workflow; who would pay (funeral homes are small, states procure EDRS from a few vendors)
technical_unlock: Physician-side mobile signing with automated reminders and escalation to the medical examiner is feasible but requires integration with state EDRS, which is procurement-gated; none obvious for a solo founder without state access
why_now: States tightening electronic filing mandates (NC 2026 explicit e-filing requirement, five-day window) raise the stakes of physician non-response
existing_solutions: State EDRS platforms (e.g., NCDAVE, CA-EDRS), funeral home software (Passare, SRS, Osiris), medical examiner escalation
